title: Schrödinger's cat
reading: In 1935, Professor Schrödinger will publish a long essay on 'the present situation in quantum mechanics'. In it: a cat is shut in a steel chamber with a small amount of radioactive substance, a Geiger counter, a hammer and a flask of poison. If within an hour one atom decays, the counter discharges, the hammer breaks the flask, and the cat dies. If one takes the wave function of the whole system literally, after an hour it contains the living and the dead cat mixed in equal parts. The uncertainty of the atom, he writes, has been transformed into an uncertainty of something we can see. The same year he names the property of the joint wave function discussed by Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen: in German, Verschränkung; in English, entanglement.
detail: Schrödinger intended the cat as a reductio of reading ψ as a description of reality while allowing it to 'blur' macroscopic states. Einstein, in correspondence the same summer, had proposed a keg of gunpowder that after a year is described by a mixture of exploded and unexploded.

claim.label: My own reductio
claim.summary: Schrödinger, shown his own later argument. The argument is documented; its reception by his 1927 self is inference.
voice: I see what I will have done. I have taken the uncertainty of the atom and joined it to something we can see. If the wave describes reality, then after an hour it describes a cat that is neither alive nor dead. No one believes that. So either the wave does not describe reality, or it is incomplete. I have been saying something like this for two years; this makes it impossible to ignore.
claim.reasoning: Linearity carries microscopic indefiniteness into macroscopic objects.

historical.note: Schrödinger published the argument in Naturwissenschaften in November–December 1935.

claim.label: My keg of gunpowder
claim.summary: Einstein welcomed the argument, having proposed a keg-of-gunpowder version in his own letter to Schrödinger. Documented for 1935; applied to the 1927 Einstein by inference.
voice: Good. I would have said it with a keg of gunpowder: after a year the wave describes a mixture of exploded and not exploded. No one thinks the real state of the keg is like that. So the wave is not a description of the real state. It is a description of our knowledge — and then it is incomplete.
claim.reasoning: Macroscopic objects have definite states; ψ that blurs them is not a complete description.

historical.note: Einstein wrote to Schrödinger on 8 August 1935 with the gunpowder example.

claim.label: The counter is the observation
claim.summary: Inference from Bohr's position: the registration by the counter is an irreversible, classically described event; the question of the cat does not arise in his framework. No documented response by Bohr to the cat.
voice: The paradox arises only if one applies the wave to the cat and the counter as though they were atomic objects. The counter's discharge is a registration, an irreversible event that we describe in classical terms. The observation is complete at that point. There is no half-dead cat in any description we are entitled to use.
claim.reasoning: Classical description of the apparatus; irreversibility of registration.

claim.label: The wave is our knowledge
claim.summary: Inference from Heisenberg's 1927 view of ψ as a summary of possible observations.
voice: Nothing in the chamber is half dead. The wave summarises what we can expect when we open it — a probability for each result. Schrödinger is still treating the wave as a thing. Once one stops, the paradox disappears.
claim.reasoning: ψ is not a physical state of the cat.

claim.label: Probability, not a blurred cat
voice: I would read the wave of the chamber as I read the wave of a scattered electron: it gives a probability for each result. The cat is alive or dead with certain probabilities. Whether anything more must be said about the moment of decay — I admit that is the uncomfortable part.

claim.label: The counter works
claim.summary: Speculative. Curie has no documented view; her experimental practice suggests she would insist on what the counter actually records.
voice: I will only say that every Geiger counter I have used either clicks or does not. If the theory describes something else before the click, that is a question for the theorists — and perhaps one for the cat.
claim.reasoning: Speculative voice, grounded only in experimental practice.
